purpose: Omacetaxine is used to treat a type of blood cancer called chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). It is specifically used when other leukemia medicines, like imatinib or dasatinib, have stopped working or are no longer tolerated. It helps to slow or stop the growth of cancer cells in your blood and bone marrow.
how_it_works: Think of cancer cells as factories that keep making harmful proteins to help them grow and survive. Omacetaxine works by blocking the machinery inside those cancer cells that makes these dangerous proteins. Without those proteins, the cancer cells can no longer grow and they eventually die off. Importantly, it works in a different way than most other leukemia drugs, so it can still work even when other treatments have failed.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include low blood cell counts (which can make you tired, increase your risk of infection, or cause easy bruising and bleeding), injection site redness or irritation, diarrhea, nausea, fatigue, fever, and hair thinning. Many patients also experience headache or swelling in their hands or feet.
warnings: This medicine can seriously lower your blood cell counts, so your doctor will do regular blood tests to monitor you closely. Because of this, you may be at higher risk for serious infections or bleeding — let your doctor know right away if you have a fever, unusual bruising, or bleeding. This drug should NOT be used if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment. It is given as an injection under the skin, so never try to administer it without proper training.
typical_dosing: Omacetaxine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually twice a day for 14 days in a row, followed by a rest period — this 28-day cycle repeats. Once your cancer is under control, the dosing schedule may be reduced to twice a day for 7 days every 28 days. Your doctor will adjust the schedule based on how your body responds and how your blood counts look.
